prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction and experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators.

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED (B020) and I still think it is a clean discovery of a new regime, but after reading the ballots I move my preferred configuration to the topological insulator candidate (B018), which I ranked third. It is the one candidate that is supported across the committee by a wide margin: five of eight members place it in their top three or four, and it is the only shortlisted item with two first places and no member who finds it premature. The physics is a genuine discovery of nature: a prediction of a new class of insulator, the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state, followed by an experiment in HgTe quantum wells that saw edge conduction of the predicted size, then two decades of independent confirmation in transport, ARPES and STM. The theory-then-experiment arc is exactly the pattern I trust, and the discovery is what is being rewarded, not an application. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a coherent three-person split from the supplied names. My own field gives me a reason to hold back on B020 specifically: a second superconducting-circuit prize one year after the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, in a field in which I am personally embedded, is a decision where my judgement should carry less weight.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation about B018 is attribution. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp's group to look in HgTe is not in the credited set, and Shoucheng Zhang died in 2018, so a prize that credits the experiment without the proposal that guided it needs careful wording, as does the 3D case (Fu, Moore, Hasan). The practical impact is also still modest, and I am outside my area here and defer to the condensed-matter members on whether the quantum spin Hall effect or the 3D topological insulator is the more decisive step. Against my own B020: the proposal and first strong-coupling experiment are shared among five people, Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff cannot all be honoured, and the overlap with the 2025 prize is real, so I cannot call B020 the obvious choice with a clear conscience.

responses.point: Ranks B018 first as a clean, verified discovery with a theory-to-experiment arc, based on band theory and measurable edge and surface states, while noting that the BHZ proposal and the 3D ARPES work are not covered by the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this, and Olle's point that recognition is arguably overdue is persuasive. I would go one step further on the credit problem. The BHZ proposal is the specific reason Molenkamp looked at HgTe, so the citation should name the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation rather than topological insulators in general; otherwise the 3D work outside the three names looks like an omission rather than a boundary. I would like Olle to say whether he sees the 2D quantum spin Hall effect as a self-contained discovery that can stand without the 3D materials.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks (B041) first as the clearest new measurement method, with record 1e-18 uncertainties and several independent labs, and ranks circuit QED sixth because the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits already honours part of that lineage.
responses.response: Stefan's timing objection to B020 is fair and I concede it, which is part of why I moved off my own first choice. I disagree somewhat about B041 being clearly ahead of B018. The lattice clock is mature and excellent, but its fundamental-physics output so far is constraints rather than discoveries, and the committee has already recognised frequency combs in 2005 and ion clocks in 2012, so the novelty has to be argued. I keep B041 as my first alternative because the two-name credit is clean and the result is robust across laboratories, which are properties I value. He is right that Blais is the lead author of the 2004 proposal and could replace Girvin in a circuit QED trio.

responses.point: Ranks B041 first and B010 second, valuing precision atomic physics that is confirmed across many laboratories, and ranks B018 fourth with the caveat that the credited trio leaves out key contributors such as Zhang, Fu and Hasan.
responses.response: I share Eva's caution about the incompleteness of the B018 credit and think it is the main point to settle in later rounds. On B010 I disagree about priority, because five credited names cannot be reduced to three without leaving out Cirac, Greiner or Dalibard, and I find it hard to say whether Jaksch-Zoller or the Greiner-Bloch experiment is the decisive step. For this reason I rank B010 below both B018 and B041, even though I ranked it second at the opening. Where we agree is that B041 is the most robust of the metrology candidates.

responses.point: Ranks fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B032) first as a simple, universal and provable set of results, and ranks B018 second with the observation that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D work leave a gap in the credit.
responses.response: Bernhard's framing of B032 as a general rule that explains many messy systems appeals to me, but I would hold it back for now because the supplied credit is contested among Evans, Gallavotti-Cohen, Jarzynski, Crooks, Kurchan and Seifert, and only one member ranks it. I would like to hear how he separates the Jarzynski equality from the Evans-Searles and Crooks relations in a three-person citation. His second-place ranking of B018 together with the same attribution concern is where we agree, and I take it as a sign that the gap is shared and should be addressed in the citation wording.

responses.point: Ranks kilonovae (B045) first and IceCube (B016) second, valuing discoveries confirmed by nature with clear clues, but notes that a single credited name for IceCube is unusual for a collaboration of that size.
responses.response: I accept Ulf's principle that discoveries confirmed by nature should lead and that B018 meets it, but I would not follow him to B016 as a stand-alone single-name prize. His own point about a single laureate for a collaboration of hundreds is the strongest argument against it, and the individual source associations are still at a modest significance. I defer to him and to Mark on neutrino astronomy and kilonovae because they are outside my expertise, but I would want to see a credible multi-person credit before I would support B016 or B045.

uncertainties: Whether the credit for B018 can be worded to cover the BHZ proposal and the HgTe observation without naming people beyond the three-laureate limit.
How much weight the committee should give a second superconducting-circuit prize one year after 2025, and whether the time gap makes B020 premature as a separate subject.
Which of Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff would be the fair three if B020 were advanced.
Whether B041 is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes to stand alone.
statement.conflict_note: I have a specific connection to B020. I am director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with the superconducting-circuit community at Chalmers, and circuit QED is the platform of that programme, so I should not take a lead role in deciding that candidate. I also have a lesser connection to the broader circuit-quantum-physics field through my own microwave quantum optics work and my Chalmers colleagues, and I have been in contact with the 2025 laureates as guest researchers there. I have no specific connection to B018, B041 or the other shortlisted candidates apparent from my profile.
